gummy-smile-botox.summary: Botulinum toxin in the upper lip muscles lowers the lip line so less gum shows when you smile; the effect lasts months.

quick.overview:
Gummy smile Botox is used by people who want less gum showing when they smile. Small amounts of botulinum toxin go into the muscles that lift the upper lip, so the lip rises less and the teeth take up more of the smile.

The toxin blocks nerve signals to those muscles, which lowers the lip line within days. Many small registered trials have compared injection sites and doses, guidance methods and combinations with surgery. Wikipedia reports an average duration of roughly six months.
quick.how: It is a clinic treatment given by a trained clinician, usually a short visit. The lowered lip line appears within days, and people repeat it when the effect fades. Some combine it with gum or lip surgery when the gum line is also part of the cause. Gummy smile is generally an off-label use.
quick.risks: Described effects include weakness of nearby muscles, bruising and headache, and the smile can look different while the toxin is active. It is a prescription product administered by clinicians, and the result wears off, so it is temporary.

angle.text: Botulinum toxin in the upper lip muscles is used by people who want less gum showing when they smile. The lip rises less, and the lowered lip line is visible within days. The result is temporary, and many small trials have measured it.

crown-lengthening-gingivectomy.summary: Dental surgery that trims gum, and sometimes bone, to expose more tooth, giving longer-looking teeth and less gum show.

quick.overview:
Crown lengthening and gingivectomy reshape the gum line so more of each tooth shows and less gum appears when you smile. They suit gummy smiles where the gum line itself is the cause.

Gum tissue is removed in gingivectomy, and crown lengthening can also recontour the supporting bone, so the gum line sits higher on the teeth. These are standard periodontal procedures, and registered trials compare surgical, flapless, piezoelectric, laser and digitally guided methods.
quick.how: A dentist or periodontist does it in the chair, trimming or repositioning gum with bone recontouring if needed. The change in tooth display is visible once the area has healed. People often use it as one step in a wider smile plan.
quick.risks: Described drawbacks include irreversible bone loss, weakening of neighbouring teeth, pain with flap surgery, recurrence and black triangles between teeth. Bone removal cannot be undone.

angle.text: Crown lengthening and gingivectomy reshape the gum line so teeth look longer and less gum shows, used for gummy smiles where the gum line is the cause. Gum and sometimes bone are trimmed back, and the change in tooth display is visible once healed.

lip-repositioning-surgery.summary: Surgery that shortens the upper lip vestibule so the lip rises less, reducing gum show in gummy smiles from a hypermobile lip.

quick.overview:
Lip repositioning surgery is aimed at gummy smiles caused by an upper lip that rises too far. It limits how high the lip lifts, so less gum shows and the smile looks more balanced.

A strip of mucosa is removed from inside the upper lip and the lip is reattached in a lower position, which reduces the depth of the vestibule and may increase lip fullness. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis measured the short- and long-term reduction in gum display, and the research base is mainly case series and small trials.
quick.how: It is an elective procedure done by a dental or oral surgeon, with the reduced gum display visible after healing. Technique variations such as adding a myotomy are discussed in the literature. People choose it when lip movement, rather than the gum line, is the cause.
quick.risks: It is a surgical procedure with the usual healing period. Reviews and trials examine relapse, meaning the lip can drift back up over time, and technique choices that affect it.

angle.text: Lip repositioning is used for gummy smiles caused by a hypermobile upper lip. A strip of inner lip mucosa is removed and the lip reattached lower, limiting how far it rises on smiling. The reduced gum display is visible after healing.

gum-contouring-laser.summary: Laser removal of gum tissue to reshape the gum line and show more even tooth length, a laser version of gingivectomy.

quick.overview:
Laser gum contouring evens out the gum line and shows more tooth, using a dental laser instead of a scalpel to trim soft tissue. It is a laser form of gingivectomy.

The laser vaporizes and cuts gum tissue while sealing small vessels, leaving a reshaped, balanced gum line once healed. Wikipedia lists Nd:YAG, CO2 and diode lasers among those used and notes proposed benefits such as a bloodless field and minimal discomfort, based on limited evidence. Few registered studies look at it directly.
quick.how: A dentist trims the gum in a short visit, and the reshaped gum line is visible after healing. It is often used alongside other smile work such as veneers or whitening.
quick.risks: High energy settings were linked to scarring and delayed healing in animal studies. As with other gum trimming, removed tissue does not simply grow back, and the claimed advantages over a scalpel rest on limited evidence.

angle.text: Laser gum contouring is used to even out the gum line and show more tooth, as a laser version of gingivectomy. The laser trims gum tissue and the reshaped gum line is visible after healing. Few studies look at the laser technique directly.

enamel-reshaping-contouring.summary: Shaving tiny amounts of enamel to even out edges, chips and slightly long or pointed teeth; quick and subtle, with a permanent result.

quick.overview:
Enamel reshaping smooths chips, evens out edges and slightly changes the length or shape of a tooth, mostly on the front teeth. People use it for quick, subtle fixes to teeth that are almost right already.

A dentist removes a thin layer of enamel using fine diamond burs, discs, strips or lasers, then polishes the surface. The change is visible straight away. It is described as a subtle change rather than a fix for major alignment problems, and no clinical studies specific to the procedure were found.
quick.how: It is usually a single-visit treatment, and since enamel has no nerve endings it often needs no anaesthetic. People often pair it with whitening or bonding, and it is a common small step in a smile makeover.
quick.risks: Enamel does not grow back, so the change is permanent. Taking off too much can expose dentin and cause temporary sensitivity.

angle.text: Enamel reshaping is used for quick, subtle fixes to uneven edges, chips and slightly long or pointed teeth, mostly on front teeth. A dentist shaves a thin layer of enamel and polishes it, and the change is visible straight away.

dental-implants.summary: Titanium tooth roots topped with a crown that replace missing teeth with a fixed, natural-looking result and decades of survival data.

quick.overview:
Dental implants replace missing teeth with a fixed, natural-looking result. A titanium or zirconia post is set in the jawbone and topped with a crown, bridge or denture, so a gap is filled with a tooth that looks and works like the original.

The post bonds to bone through osseointegration, then supports the prosthetic tooth after healing. Reported survival is about 93 to 98 percent at five years or more in healthy tissue. On looksmaxxing forums people also ask whether implants and bone grafts can thicken the jaw or build chin projection, but reference sources describe implants as tooth replacements and do not describe such effects.
quick.how: Placement is oral surgery done in stages, with healing time before the crown is fitted. Rough surfaces and coatings are designed to speed bone attachment. People plan implants around gaps, failing teeth and the final shape of the smile.
quick.risks: Complications include infection, loosening, fracture, nerve injury and peri-implantitis (bone loss around the implant), which are more likely with smoking, poor hygiene and diabetes. It is a surgical, hard-to-reverse treatment.

angle.text: Dental implants replace missing teeth with a fixed, natural-looking result: a titanium root is set in bone and a crown fitted on top. Forum posters also ask about thickening the jaw or building up a recessed chin with implants and grafts, but that use is not described in reference sources.

crowns-and-bridges.summary: Caps and fixed bridges that rebuild damaged, discoloured or missing teeth so the smile looks complete and even.

quick.overview:
Crowns and bridges restore the shape, colour and completeness of teeth. A crown is a cap over a damaged or discoloured tooth, and a bridge fills a gap by anchoring an artificial tooth to neighbouring teeth or implants.

The tooth is shaped, an impression or digital scan is taken, and a restoration in metal, porcelain or zirconia is cemented on, often designed and milled with CAD/CAM systems. They are standard restorative dentistry and are also used cosmetically on teeth that whitening or bonding cannot fix. Typical survival is reported at about 90 to 95 percent over 5 to 10 years.
quick.how: Treatment takes a couple of visits, with a temporary restoration in between. The finished look is visible once fitted. Restorations typically need replacing after around 10 years.
quick.risks: Preparation permanently removes tooth structure. Reported problems include decay at the margins, porcelain chipping, debonding, gum irritation, wear of opposing teeth and nickel allergy.

angle.text: Crowns restore damaged teeth and bridges fill gaps from missing teeth, so the smile looks complete and uniform. Caps or bridges are fitted over or between teeth, and the restored look is visible once fitted. The methods are long established.

smile-makeover-digital-smile-design.summary: A planned bundle of cosmetic dental work designed around your whole smile and previewed digitally first.

quick.overview:
A smile makeover redesigns the smile as a whole by combining treatments such as whitening, bonding, veneers, crowns, gum contouring and orthodontics into one plan. The aim is a changed colour, shape, size, alignment and display of teeth and gums.

Digital smile design is the planning step: photos and software, or wax mock-ups, preview the proposed look and apply proportion guidelines such as tooth width-to-length ratios. Clinicians assess facial features, tooth display and the gum line, then combine procedures to match the design, sometimes producing restorations with CAD/CAM. No clinical studies specific to smile makeovers were found.
quick.how: It usually runs as a multi-step programme with a design consultation, a preview or trial mock-up, then the chosen treatments in sequence. Timelines depend on which procedures are included.
quick.risks: Veneers and crowns usually require permanent removal of tooth structure. Cosmetic dentistry is not an ADA-recognised specialty, and critics raise overtreatment and marketing concerns. Costs are typically high.

angle.text: A smile makeover bundles whitening, bonding, veneers, crowns, gum contouring and orthodontics into one planned redesign, often previewed with digital smile design first. The new smile is visible once the work is complete.

smile-training-smile-mirror-practice.summary: Rehearsing your smile in a mirror or on camera to find a more natural, flattering expression, at no cost.

quick.overview:
Smile training means practising your smile, usually in front of a mirror or camera, to find an expression that looks more natural and flattering in person and in photos. It is free and needs no equipment.

People practise controlling the facial muscles, for example engaging the muscles around the eyes as in a Duchenne smile. Related research covers smile types and the facial feedback hypothesis, the idea that expressions influence emotion; a 2016 multi-lab replication did not reproduce a classic 1988 finding, while a later meta-analysis reported a small effect overall. No trials of the practice itself for attractiveness were found.
quick.how: There is no formal protocol. People rehearse short sessions in a mirror, review photos or video of themselves, and keep the expressions that look best, often combining it with dental or grooming changes.
quick.risks: No documented harms were found for the practice itself.

angle.text: People practise smiling in a mirror or on camera to find a more natural, flattering expression for daily life and photos. Rehearsal builds control of the facial muscles, so the expression comes more easily. It is free to try, and no trials of the practice itself were located.

smile-maxxing.summary: Community shorthand for optimising your smile, from whitening and alignment to gums, lips and how you express it.

quick.overview:
Smile maxxing is a looksmaxxing term for making your smile look better. It covers dental changes such as whitening, alignment and cosmetic dentistry, gum and lip work, and the way the smile is expressed.

Dentally, it involves procedures that change tooth colour, shape and position. Expressively, it concerns which facial muscles are used, for example whether a smile engages the eyes (Duchenne smile). It has no formal definition, and no published research uses the term; it overlaps with cosmetic dentistry and smile training.
quick.how: People usually start with the basics such as whitening and hygiene, then add alignment, cosmetic dentistry or gum work, and practise expression in a mirror or on camera. Timelines depend on the route chosen.
quick.risks: Risks depend on the method. Dental procedures such as veneers can involve irreversible tooth reduction, while expression practice carries little reported risk.

angle.text: Smile maxxing is a community umbrella term for improving the smile through whitening, alignment, cosmetic dentistry, gum and lip work, or better expression. Better teeth, gums and expression add up to a smile that looks more attractive. The term has no formal definition.

snap-on-smile.summary: A thin removable appliance that fits over your teeth for an instantly straighter, brighter-looking smile while worn.

quick.overview:
Snap-On Smile is a thin removable appliance that fits over your existing teeth and gives an even, bright-looking set of front teeth the moment it goes in. It is a branded dental product from DenMat, and the term is also used loosely online for removable fake veneers.

It is a tooth-borne overdenture, reported to be made from acetal resin, that covers the teeth without altering them. Dental literature describes it as a temporary esthetic option, documented in case reports on older or medically complex patients, enamel disorders and implant provisionals. No trials have assessed it.
quick.how: It is fitted by a dentist from impressions of your teeth and worn over them, then taken out for eating and cleaning. People use it as a temporary or provisional smile, for example during other dental treatment.
quick.risks: Reports note the teeth can look too large in people with high smile lines or altered gums. It is described as temporary and does not change the teeth underneath.

angle.text: Snap-on smile appliances cover the existing teeth with a removable shell, giving an instantly even, bright-looking set of front teeth while worn. The change is immediate. Dental literature describes it as a temporary esthetic option documented in case reports.

fake-tooth-caps-press-on-veneers.summary: Removable cosmetic covers that change the look of your front teeth instantly, with no dental work.

quick.overview:
Press-on veneers and fake tooth caps are removable shells that sit over the front teeth to change their apparent shape or shade. The change is visible as soon as they are placed, for a more even, brighter smile.

They are non-prescription products and differ from dentist-made veneers, which are thin layers of composite or porcelain bonded to the tooth. The shell sits over the natural teeth, usually without bonding or tooth preparation. No published studies on the retail products were found.
quick.how: People buy them over the counter, fit them over their teeth at home and wear them for photos, events or short periods, then take them out. They are used as a temporary try-out of a look.
quick.risks: Safety and fit have not been studied in published research, and professional veneer literature does not cover these products.

angle.text: Press-on veneers are used to change the apparent shape or shade of the teeth for a more even, brighter smile. The cover is placed over the front teeth and the change is visible as soon as they are on. No studies on these non-prescription covers have been published.

diy-braces-with-rubber-bands-paperclips.summary: Improvised home tooth-moving with bands or wire, discussed as a low-cost route to straighter teeth.

quick.overview:
DIY braces means trying to straighten teeth at home with household rubber bands or bent wire, as a cheap alternative to orthodontic treatment. The goal is a straighter-looking smile.

The idea is that improvised bands or wire apply force to move teeth. Professional braces apply controlled forces that clinicians adjust over months. The appeal comes from personal accounts and home attempts, and no published research examines the practice.
quick.how: People describe wrapping or looping bands or wire around teeth to pull them together or into line, with no clinician involved and no set schedule.
quick.risks: It has not been studied. The orthodontic reference describes decay risk and relapse even in supervised treatment, and the practice is unsupervised.

angle.text: People discuss improvised bands and bent wire as a low-cost way to straighten teeth without orthodontic treatment, aiming for a straighter smile. The idea is that home-made tension shifts teeth into line. It rests on personal accounts, and no research on the practice exists.

diy-gap-bands.summary: Small elastic bands placed around front teeth at home to try to close a gap between them.

quick.overview:
DIY gap bands are small elastic bands that people place around front teeth hoping to close a gap (diastema) and get a more uniform smile without visiting a dentist.

The band is meant to apply inward force so the teeth drift together. In clinics, such forces are applied by supervised appliances, including elastics and springs. The appearance benefit is based on personal accounts, and no research on the home practice was found.
quick.how: People loop the band around the two teeth beside the gap and leave it in place, with no clinician checking progress.
quick.risks: It has not been studied in published research, and it is done without supervision.

angle.text: Users place small elastic bands around front teeth hoping to close a gap (diastema) and get a more uniform smile without a dentist. The band is meant to pull the teeth together. The benefit is based on personal accounts, and no studies on the method exist.

chewing-hard-foods-for-jaw.summary: Chewing tough or hard foods to build the jaw muscles for a more defined jawline.

quick.overview:
Some people chew hard or tough foods hoping to enlarge the masseter muscles and get a more defined jawline. Proponents tie it to the idea that chewing grows the jaw muscles.

The masseter is a strong chewing muscle that can enlarge with habitual heavy use such as clenching, grinding or constant gum chewing. No studies were found testing hard-food chewing as a way to change facial appearance.
quick.how: People add tough items to their routine and chew them regularly, often alongside other jaw and posture habits. Any visible change would build gradually, like other muscle training.
quick.risks: Hard-food chewing is listed among habits suggested to be associated with temporomandibular (jaw joint) disorders, though evidence is limited.

angle.text: Forum posters chew tough or hard foods to build the masseter muscles and get a more defined jawline. It draws on the general principle that muscles grow with load, and the masseter can enlarge with habitual heavy use. Its effect on facial appearance has not been tested.

jawline-exerciser-jawzrsize.summary: A resistance chewing device marketed to strengthen the jaw muscles and define the jawline.

quick.overview:
Jawline exercisers such as Jawzrsize are handheld devices you bite or chew against with resistance, marketed to strengthen the jaw muscles and give a more defined jawline.

The pitch borrows from muscle-training logic: resistance chewing loads the masseter, which can enlarge with habitual heavy use. No published research on the products or their effect on facial appearance was found.
quick.how: Users bite into the device in repeated sets as a daily routine, in the same way they would train any other muscle, and compare photos over weeks or months.
quick.risks: Repetitive jaw habits are suggested to be associated with jaw disorders, with limited evidence.

angle.text: Jawline exercisers like Jawzrsize are marketed to users who want stronger, larger jaw muscles and a sharper-looking jawline. You bite against resistance, following muscle-training logic. No studies on the product or its effect on facial appearance exist.

orthodontic-extractions-debate.summary: The long-running split over removing teeth to align the rest, and how each choice may affect your smile and profile.

quick.overview:
Orthodontic choices shape both the smile and the facial profile, which is why looksmaxxers follow this debate. Orthodontists sometimes remove teeth, most often premolars, to relieve crowding or change the lip profile, and the question of whether to has been argued since the early 1900s.

Mainstream orthodontics treats extraction as one option chosen case by case, based on crowding, bite and profile. Orthotropic proponents, following John Mew, regard extractions as potentially harmful to facial growth and favour expansion; the orthotropic view is not supported by mainstream professional bodies. In looksmaxxing circles the argument is usually framed around the claim that extractions shrink the jaws and flatten the face, and published evidence on this is limited and contested.
quick.how: People weigh the options in consultations: extraction plans create space so remaining teeth can be aligned or retracted, while non-extraction plans such as expansion make room another way. Many seek second opinions before choosing.
quick.risks: Extractions are irreversible and carry general surgical risks. Non-extraction plans such as expansion also have limits and relapse risk. Community members often describe fear of a changed profile.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers follow this debate because orthodontic choices shape both the smile and the facial profile. Premolar removal or arch expansion changes tooth alignment and how the profile sits. One camp holds extractions flatten the face and favours expansion, while orthodontic history shows both approaches in use.

invisalign-attachments-chewies.summary: Small bonded bumps and soft bite cylinders that help clear aligners grip and seat for straighter teeth.

quick.overview:
Clear aligners are plastic trays that move teeth in stages toward a straighter smile. Attachments and chewies are two accessories that help them work: attachments are small tooth-colored composite shapes bonded to teeth, and chewies are soft cylinders you bite on to press the tray fully onto the teeth.

Because plastic is less rigid than metal, attachments give the tray something to push against so it can rotate or pull down teeth. Chewies use biting force to seat the tray and close small gaps. Aligners typically move teeth about 0.25 to 0.33 mm per stage, are worn around 22 hours a day, and treatment averages about 13.5 months. Chewies are informal and have no dedicated trial.
quick.how: Attachments are placed by a clinician as part of the treatment plan. Chewies are used by patients for a few minutes at a time, mostly when a new tray feels loose.
quick.risks: More attachments can make aligners look less discreet. Aligners in general are considered less effective than braces for rotations, extrusion and front-to-back jaw discrepancies, and relapse is reported.

angle.text: Attachments and chewies are accessories that help clear aligners seat and rotate teeth, supporting a straighter smile over the course of treatment. Attachments give the plastic tray something to grip, so it moves teeth more precisely. Attachments are described in dental sources; chewies are informal.

retainer-wear-nightly.summary: Wearing a retainer at night after braces or aligners to hold your teeth in their straightened positions.

quick.overview:
Retainers keep a straightened smile straight. After teeth are moved they tend to drift back toward their old positions, and many orthodontists advise nightly wear for years after full-time wear. In looksmaxxing circles it is the way to keep braces or aligner results.

Retainers resist relapse forces from recoil of the periodontal fibres, soft-tissue pressure, the bite and continued growth. Orthodontic sources describe a lifelong risk of relapse, with more than half of patients showing some reversion within 10 years.
quick.how: Removable types, Hawley or vacuum-formed, are worn at set times, usually overnight; fixed types are wires bonded behind the front teeth. One overview suggests about six months of full-time wear followed by nighttime wear for many years, and the schedule is set by the treating orthodontist.
quick.risks: Poor cleaning can cause plaque, cavities and gum inflammation. Clear retainers worn while eating can trap sugary or acidic substances, and hot water can distort them. Grinding can break them quickly.

angle.text: People who have finished braces or aligners wear retainers at night to keep the straight smile they paid for. The retainer holds tooth positions and limits relapse. Orthodontic sources describe a lifelong relapse risk, with over half of patients showing some reversion within ten years.

wisdom-tooth-removal.summary: Surgical removal of third molars, routine when they are impacted and discussed by looksmaxxers for crowding and jaw development.

quick.overview:
Wisdom teeth, the third molars, usually erupt between about 17 and 21. When they lack room they can become impacted, and they are commonly removed to treat or prevent decay, gum infection or pain. Some looksmaxxers also discuss removal as a way to protect front-tooth alignment or relate it to jaw development.

Some clinicians have removed them to prevent crowding, which is disputed: research has found no agreed view that wisdom teeth cause lower incisor crowding, and the jaw-shape link is forum theory. NICE guidance (2000) and the American Public Health Association oppose prophylactic removal, and a 2020 Cochrane review found evidence insufficient to settle the question.
quick.how: Removal is an oral surgery procedure, often with a flap and bone removal for impacted teeth. Swelling and pain after surgery are the common effects studied in trials of drugs and techniques, and people typically plan recovery time.
quick.risks: Removing lower third molars can damage the inferior alveolar nerve temporarily or permanently, reported in about 1 in 85 patients. Other risks include dry socket, swelling and infection.

angle.text: Wisdom teeth are routinely removed when impacted, and some looksmaxxers also discuss removal as a way to protect front-tooth alignment or relate it to jaw development. The crowding link is disputed among clinicians, and the jaw-shape link is based on forum theory.
